before.label: Frantz Fanon
before.description: Analyzes colonial domination through racialized experience, psychic injury, and struggles for liberation. A psychiatrist and political theorist whose work supplies historians with questions about subject formation, violence, and the limits of national liberation; his arguments are not confined to individual psychology.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Black Skin, White Masks (French original 1952); The Wretched of the Earth (French original 1961). Later English editions have different publication dates.

after.label: Frantz Fanon
after.description: Analyzes colonial domination through racialized experience, psychic injury, and struggles for liberation. A psychiatrist and political theorist whose work supplies historians with questions about subject formation, violence, and the limits of national liberation; his arguments are not confined to individual psychology.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Black Skin, White Masks (French original 1952); The Wretched of the Earth (French original 1961). Later English editions have different publication dates.
after.scope_note: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) treats racialized experience through psychological and social explanation; its introduction names Freud while insisting on sociogeny. The Wretched of the Earth (1961) combines liberation strategy, criticism of elite nationalism and psychiatric cases. These are connected inquiries, not one invariant doctrine or membership in psychohistory. Gendered and regional generalizations require critical reading.

before.label: Walter Rodney
before.description: Explains African underdevelopment as an historical relationship shaped by slavery, colonial extraction, and capitalism. His scholarship joins African and Caribbean history to Pan-African politics and popular education. Dependency analysis captures part of his work, not its full historical and political range.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).

after.label: Walter Rodney
after.description: Explains underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of slavery, colonial extraction and capitalism. Regional African research, Guyanese labor history and popular education give his work distinct scales and audiences. His account of systemic constraints also investigates changing societies; dependency analysis captures only part of his scholarship and politics.
after.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).
after.scope_note: A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800 (1970, from a 1966 thesis) reconstructs regional change; The Groundings with My Brothers (1969) concerns political education; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) offers a didactic synthesis. A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905 (posthumous, 1981) examines labor and racial divisions. His 1975 Marxism lecture distinguishes method from fixed European conclusions. James’s later strategic criticism coexists with formative intellectual exchange.

before.label: Nationalism studies
before.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.

added.relationship: Rodney adapts materialist method to historical time and place
added.evidence_note: His 1975 lecture explicitly separates method from conclusions about nineteenth-century Europe. This is his account of a conceptual resource, not a claim that African/Caribbean history derives wholly from European theory.

added.relationship: Upper Guinea research connects regional change and Atlantic slave trading
added.evidence_note: The 1966 thesis abstract identifies European and intra-African forces; the 1970 book contributes regional scholarship. This does not certify every argument of the unread book or make Africans a single responding actor.
added.map_label: Upper Guinea: regional and Atlantic relations

added.relationship: Guyanese working people become subjects of differentiated labor history
added.evidence_note: The posthumous 1981 book addresses immigration, race, class, resistance and accommodation. Mapping it here identifies substantive social history, not membership in a unified school. Publisher-level support retains its limits.
added.map_label: Guyana: labor, race and class divisions

added.relationship: James criticizes Rodney’s political preparation for taking power
added.evidence_note: The 1981 memorial lecture offers a strategic disagreement alongside admiration. James’s diagnosis is not adopted as an explanation of the assassination or proof of what Rodney did not know. This differs from the formative influence in edge_156.

added.relationship: Fanon distinguishes popular emancipation from elite succession
added.evidence_note: His 1961 criticism of the intermediary national bourgeoisie and emphasis on political participation supply an earlier conceptual resource for studying nationalism. This is an editorial connection, not demonstrated influence on every later nationalism theorist.

before.relationship: contributes analyses of colonial domination and liberation
before.evidence_note: An intellectual contribution by a theorist and psychiatrist, not a claim that all anti-colonial history is Fanonian. Colonial domination and liberation are Fanon’s contribution; his analysis is distinct from economic histories by Williams or Rodney.

after.relationship: contributes analyses of colonial domination and liberation
after.evidence_note: Psychiatric inquiry and liberation politics intersect without defining all anti-colonial history. The checked 1961 passages criticize elite succession and stress participation; Fanon’s regional and gendered claims remain open to criticism.

before.relationship: provides psychoanalytic resources reworked in an analysis of racialized colonial experience
before.evidence_note: Psychoanalysis is one resource among several; this does not place Fanon within the psychohistory subfield. Fanon reworks psychoanalysis through racialized colonial experience rather than applying it unchanged.

after.relationship: provides psychoanalytic resources reworked in an analysis of racialized colonial experience
after.evidence_note: Fanon explicitly discusses Freud in the 1952 introduction, extending explanation from individual development to sociogeny. Psychoanalysis remains one resource among several; this does not place Fanon within psychohistory or imply unchanged application.

before.relationship: develops an African historical account of relational underdevelopment
before.evidence_note: Represents a substantive contribution, not the absorption of all Rodney’s work into an umbrella school. Rodney offers a relational account of African underdevelopment; this does not identify all African history with dependency theory.

after.relationship: develops an African historical account of relational underdevelopment
after.evidence_note: Rodney’s checked excerpt supplies unequal power; Wallerstein’s 1986 reading distinguishes systemic constraint from simple stagnation. That sympathetic interpretation does not settle disputes over African agency or absorb all Rodney’s work into dependency theory.

before.relationship: connects historical research with Pan-African politics and popular education
before.evidence_note: Groundings provides a route beyond academic dependency theory. Research, teaching, and Pan-African political activity intersect in Rodney’s work; the intellectual and institutional roles differ.
